title: PAO proposes aligning compensation for unjustly detained with minimum wage
summary: The Public Attorney"s Office (PAO) has recommended raising the compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes. It said the increase should be pegged to the minimum…

blocks.text: The Public Attorney’s Office (PAO) has recommended raising the compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes. It said the increase should be pegged to the minimum wage.

During a hearing on Thursday, the House Committee on Justice tackled House Bills 2337 and 2421, which seek to raise compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment, detention, and violent crimes and allocate funds for the payouts by amending Republic Act (RA) No. 7309.
The Board of Claims said compensation for victims of unjust imprisonment is currently set at P1,000 per month, capped at P60,000.
Lawyer Noliver Barrido of PAO said the current compensation falls far short of the daily minimum wage that an unjustly imprisoned individual could have earned had they not been detained.
“Ang PAO ay naniniwala na masyadong mababa po ang kompensasyon, ‘yung panukalang P5,000 o P10,000,” Barrido said.
(PAO believes that the proposed compensation of P5,000 or P10,000 is still too low.)

“Kung titingnan po natin kung ipe-pair po sa P5,000 kada buwan ang halaga po ng kompensasyon, ang ibig sabihin po sa isang araw o 24 hours na pagkakakulong ng isang tao ang ibabayad po ng estado sa kaniya ay P167,” he added.
(If we look at pairing the compensation at P5,000 per month, that means for one day or 24 hours of a person’s imprisonment, the state will only pay them P167.)
Even with a P10,000 monthly rate, PAO said this would translate to P333.33 per day, which remains well below the P755 daily minimum wage in the National Capital Region.
PAO said it also disagrees with setting a ceiling or maximum limit on the compensation.

“So ang isang manggagawa na papasok nang 8 hours at 20 days sa isang buwan ay kikita ng P15,000 mahigit. Mas mataas po ito as compared po sa compensation na ibibgay natin sa mga biktima ng maling pagpaparatang o bayolenteng krimen,” Barrido said.
(A worker who puts in eight hours a day for 20 days a month earns over P15,000. That is higher compared to the compensation we would be giving to victims of false accusations or violent crimes.)

“Hindi po categorical na sinabi sa aming position paper pero ginawa po naming batayan yung minimum wage rate po, at sana po ay i-peg po sa min wage rate ang bayad sa akusadong ng maling pinaratangan at dapat po siya mabayaran ang kada araw ng pagkakakulong at wala pong ceiling,” he added.

(It wasn’t categorically stated in our position paper, but we used the minimum wage rate as our basis, and we hope the payment to someone wrongly accused will be pegged to the minimum wage rate, paid for every day of imprisonment, and without a ceiling.)
The Commission on Human Rights and Gabriela Representative Sarah Elago both agreed with PAO’s suggestion.
Elago said even the P10,000 rate is far from a living wage, pointing out that the compensation should be enough to support a victim’s family.
Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro, the panel’s chairperson, said that while their proposals are understandable, budget limitations must also be acknowledged.

“We understand the point of PAO and the CHR that we have to consider the amount of minimum wage, as well as their leaning towards removing the cap. But let’s acknowledge also that budget limitations is real,” Luistro said.
During the hearing, the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR) said the law mandates it to allot 1% of its net income to the Victims Compensation Program.
While the agency agreed to the higher compensation, it opposed increasing the percentage share it contributes to the program.
PAGCOR said it has reservations about any corresponding hike in its statutory contribution, citing potential effects on the agency’s other mandated obligations.
Luistro said a catch-all provision will instead be introduced, granting the Board of Claims the prerogative to award compensation beyond the cap, provided it is justified.

“So perhaps in proposed catch-all provision, kung meron mga extraordinary cases na mare-receive ang Board of Claims, we can suggest in that catch-all provision to consider the minimum wage, to consider removing the cap for extraordinary claims of victims of violent crimes and unjust detention and accusation,” Luistro said.
She added that adjusting PAGCOR's 1% contribution would require a separate legislative measure.
The justice panel subsequently approved the bills amending Republic Act No. 7309.

Among the approved provisions is granting the Board of Claims the authority to award compensation exceeding the prescribed maximum limit in exceptional cases, based on the gravity of the injury and other relevant circumstances of the claimant.

“Taking into consideration the peculiar circumstances of each case, the gravity and extent of the injury or damage suffered, the duration and consequences of the unjust imprisonment or detention, the actual losses and expenses incurred and such relevant factors as may be necessary to ensure the compensation awarded is just, reasonable and commensurate with the harm suffered by the claimant,” read the catch-all provision presented by panel Vice Chairperson Rep. Bel Zamora.
The provision also directs the Board of Claims to state in writing the factual and legal basis whenever it awards compensation exceeding the prescribed maximum amount. —LDF, GMA News
